title: Muslim Ban Executive Order - Religious Discrimination
description_short: Just seven days into his presidency, Trump signed Executive Order 13769, banning entry to the United States for citizens of seven majority-Muslim countries
description_medium: On January 27, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769, temporarily restricting entry for nationals of seven Muslim-majority countries and suspending refugee admissions. The order set a 90-day visa suspension for Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen; paused the U.S. refugee program for 120 days; and indefinitely suspended Syrian refugee admissions. It also capped refugee admissions for 2017 at 50,000.
description_long: Trump signed Executive Order 13769 one week after taking office. It combined a temporary suspension of entry for nationals of Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen with a pause in refugee admissions. The order suspended the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program for 120 days, indefinitely halted Syrian refugee admissions, and set a 50,000-person ceiling for refugee admissions in 2017, below the 110,000 limit set by the prior administration. Some visa categories, including diplomats and United Nations officials, were excluded, and officials could consider case-by-case exceptions. The order also directed priority for religious minorities facing persecution; Trump separately singled out Christians in Syria in an interview. The measure therefore affected both travelers seeking entry and people waiting for refugee resettlement, with different time limits and exceptions applying to each group. The BBC account describes protests and confusion around implementation as the order took effect. This description concerns the policy and its immediate rollout; the order’s stated humanitarian exception did not change the nationality-based restrictions faced by travelers from the seven listed countries.

title: Commutes Sentence of Hector Madrigal, Sr.
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Hector Madrigal, Sr. as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Trump commuted Hector Madrigal, Sr.’s sentence in a clemency action listed by the Justice Department. The department’s record identifies two Texas federal cases, each carrying a 20-year prison sentence and 10 years of supervised release. Both convictions were for conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute more than 1,000 kilograms of marijuana.
description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list records Trump’s January 19, 2021, commutation for Hector Madrigal, Sr. It identifies two cases in the Southern District of Texas. In both, Madrigal had been sentenced to 20 years in prison and 10 years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute more than 1,000 kilograms of marijuana. The list presents the sentences and offenses but does not explain how much prison time remained, describe the circumstances of the cases, or state why Trump selected Madrigal for clemency. A commutation changes a sentence; the department’s entry does not say the underlying convictions were vacated. The action came on the final day of Trump’s first term, when he issued clemency decisions for multiple people. The available record supports the date, recipient, two cases and listed penalties, but not an account of the decision-making process or any personal connection that may have influenced it. Those limits matter because the entry is evidence of a presidential sentence reduction, not by itself evidence of favoritism or a reason for the decision.

title: Restricts Travel from China Over COVID-19
description_short: Trump issued a proclamation suspending entry of certain travelers from China due to the coronavirus outbreak.
description_medium: On January 31, 2020, Trump issued a proclamation limiting entry by noncitizens who had been physically present in mainland China during the previous 14 days, subject to listed exceptions. The restriction took effect on February 2 as the new coronavirus outbreak was centered in China. It excluded Hong Kong and Macau from the geographic definition and formed part of the administration’s early federal response to the outbreak.
description_long: Trump’s January 31, 2020, proclamation responded to the emerging coronavirus outbreak by suspending and limiting entry for noncitizens who had been physically present in the People’s Republic of China during the 14 days before seeking to enter the United States. The measure excluded Hong Kong and Macau and contained exceptions, including for U.S. lawful permanent residents and some immediate family members, as well as specified travel categories. It took effect at 5 p.m. Eastern time on February 2. The proclamation described the outbreak as centered in China and cited concerns about transmission and risks to the country’s transportation system, infrastructure and national security. Its rule was based on recent physical presence, not simply a person’s citizenship, so it did not bar every traveler from China and could apply to noncitizens of other nationalities who had recently been there. The archived White House text documents the scope and rationale announced at the time. It does not, on its own, establish how many people were prevented from traveling or measure the policy’s effect on the spread of COVID-19.

preserved_fields.title: Restricts Travel from China Over COVID-19
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump issued a proclamation suspending entry of certain travelers from China due to the coronavirus outbreak.

title: Superseding Indictment Adds New Charges in Documents Case
description_short: Prosecutors filed a superseding indictment adding charges and a third defendant in the classified documents case, including allegations tied to surveillance footage deletion.
description_medium: On July 27, 2023, federal prosecutors filed a superseding indictment in the classified-documents case, adding three charges against Trump and naming Mar-a-Lago maintenance chief Carlos de Oliveira as a third defendant. The filing alleged that Trump and his aide Walt Nauta took part in an effort to delete surveillance footage at the Florida club during the summer of 2022. These were criminal allegations, not findings of guilt.
description_long: The July 27, 2023, superseding indictment expanded the federal case over classified documents retained at Mar-a-Lago after Trump left office. CNBC reported that prosecutors added three charges against Trump and brought a third defendant into the case: Carlos de Oliveira, the club’s maintenance chief. The new allegations included an effort during the summer of 2022 to delete surveillance footage, attributed to Trump and his valet, Walt Nauta. A superseding indictment updates the charges prosecutors ask a court to consider; it does not establish that the alleged conduct occurred. The filing therefore changed the case’s scope by adding accusations and another defendant while the earlier classified-documents charges remained pending. The available report supports the date, the added defendant, the new charges and the surveillance-footage allegation, but it does not provide a full account of each count or the later disposition of the case. The conduct described here should be read as prosecutors’ claims in a charging document, not as a verdict. The indictment’s significance at this point was procedural: it brought additional alleged obstruction-related conduct into the same prosecution.

preserved_fields.description_short: Prosecutors filed a superseding indictment adding charges and a third defendant in the classified documents case, including allegations tied to surveillance footage deletion.

title: NPR: DOJ Withheld Epstein Files Tied to Trump Accusations
description_short: An NPR investigation reported that the Justice Department withheld or removed Epstein files related to accusations involving Trump, despite a transparency law.
description_medium: NPR reported in February 2026 that dozens of pages related to allegations involving Trump were absent from the public Epstein-files database despite the Epstein Files Transparency Act. By comparing document serial numbers and case records, NPR identified 53 apparently missing pages, including FBI interview material concerning a woman who alleged abuse by Epstein as a minor and whose account also involved Trump. The allegation is not a finding of fact.
description_long: NPR’s February 2026 investigation compared serial numbers in the Justice Department’s public Epstein-files database with FBI records, emails and discovery logs. It found dozens of pages that appeared to be catalogued but not publicly available, including 53 pages of interview documents and notes related to a woman who accused Trump of sexually abusing her when she was a minor. NPR reported that FBI agents interviewed the woman four times; only the first interview, from July 24, 2019, was public, and that interview did not mention Trump. The report described her allegation, not an established finding. NPR said the missing material remained unpublished despite the Epstein Files Transparency Act and that the department had declined to answer questions about the specific records. In a letter to Congress, Attorney General Pam Bondi and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said records had not been withheld or redacted because of embarrassment, reputational harm or political sensitivity. The public-record discrepancy and the department’s response are central to the story; the available reporting does not establish why the pages were unavailable or independently prove the accusation against Trump.

preserved_fields.title: NPR: DOJ Withheld Epstein Files Tied to Trump Accusations
preserved_fields.description_short: An NPR investigation reported that the Justice Department withheld or removed Epstein files related to accusations involving Trump, despite a transparency law.
